item.title: When spike sorting matters: single-neuron identity in the quantification of neural circuits
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Suarez-Barrera, D., Encinas-Rodriguez, N., Diaz, H., Zainos, A., Bayones, L., Rossi-Pool, R.
Multiunit threshold crossings support high-performance brain-computer interfaces and preserve the low-dimensional trajectories that summarize population dynamics, raising the question of when spike sorting is still necessary. Using previously published recordings from four rhesus monkeys, we analyzed areas 3b and 1 of primary somatosensory cortex and ventral premotor cortex during a bimodal detection task, and ventral premotor cortex during an interval comparison task. From the same spikes, we built three representations: putative single units obtained with nonlinear sorting (UMAP and HDBSCAN), intermingled units obtained with linear sorting, and unsorted multiunit activity. Nonlinear sorting resolved up to three times more units than multiunit activity. In area 1, mixing discarded the periodicity information carried by phase-locked neurons, lengthened intrinsic timescales by about 40%, increased trial-to-trial variability, and raised neurometric detection thresholds by 33%. In premotor cortex, mixing reduced the task-related information recovered from the population and hid significant dimensions of its dynamics. After geometric alignment, the overall shape of population trajectories was nearly identical across representations, but distances between population states were distorted, and the approximately linear representation of interval duration saturated for longer intervals. Multiunit activity is therefore sufficient for analyses that rely on the dominant, shared structure of population activity, such as decoding, whereas analyses of single-neuron coding, variability, timescales, dimensionality, and parametric representations often require spike sorting.

item.title: The neural markers of insight problem-solving
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: SocArXiv
Emilie Caspar et al.
An “Aha!” moment corresponds to the moment the solution to a problem suddenly pops into one’s mind. The phenomenological experience of the “Aha!” moment is characterised by a feeling of suddenness and pleasure and by an increased confidence in the solution. On a cognitive level, insight problem-solving is linked to cognitive restructuring processes – a change in mental representation of information or knowledge -, and to attentional processes. In this study, we plan to use a multi-step puzzle to investigate the differences in the neural and physiological activity between insight and analytical problem-solving at each step of the solving process. We plan to record participants’ neural activity with an EEG, as well as the heart rate and skin conductance of the participants. Through an analysis of the event-related potentials after the response and time-frequency analysis before finding the answers, we expect to find markers associated with insight in frontal and parietal regions. In accordance with the previous literature, we also expect an increased heart rate for analytical problem-solving and a greater skin conductance for insight problem-solving. We also hypothesise that we will be able to find the neural markers of insights within the different steps of the puzzle, even when the solution is ultimately found analytically.

item.title: Trial history and model-derived reward prediction errors in mousevisual decisions
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Mirabedini, A., JanatAbadi, R., Khanteymoori, A.
A reward prediction error (RPE) estimated from an animal's behavior can predict its next choice. Part of this predictive value may come from information about earlier trials that a choice model could also use directly. We asked whether a model-derived RPE improves choice prediction beyond the observable history of stimuli, choices, and rewards. We analyzed 275,292 trials from 107 mice performing the International Brain Laboratory visual decision task and evaluated the main choice models on sessions that were not used for fitting. Recent choices strongly improved prediction. An RPE based on a stimulus-dependent reward expectation added a small gain beyond the preceding choice and reward, and this gain fell to near zero once the model included the preceding stimulus. When the model also summarized choices and rewards over several earlier trials, an RPE trace with the same retention parameter as the history traces did not reliably improve prediction. In simulated agents with known decision rules, a simplified version of this comparison detected an RPE-based learning rule in which choices depended on accumulated prediction errors, and did not improve prediction for an agent that used trial history directly. In mice, the state-dependent RPE and its trace added little predictive information beyond observable trial history, which limits what choice prediction alone can reveal about prediction-error learning.

item.title: Overexpression of α synuclein in Midbrain Dopamine Neurons Drives Learning Deficits in Mice
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Coutant, B., Zhuang, X., Seiler, J., Nadel, J., Romo, K., Fu, Y., Edwards, R. L., Halliday, G., Lerner, T., Nelson, A. B.
Parkinson disease (PD) is diagnosed based on core motor features. However, changes in cognitive function are often already present. Cognitive symptoms include changes in executive function, including organization, planning, multi-tasking, and flexible decision-making. These early cognitive deficits have been difficult to model and remain understudied. Here, we investigated whether AAV-based overexpression of wild-type human alpha-synuclein (syn) in midbrain dopaminergic neurons can produce deficits in learning and behavioral flexibility. We found that syn mice develop progressive impairment in basic action-outcome learning. In addition, we found that syn mice show impairments in behavioral flexibility during probabilistic reversal learning. Together, these findings demonstrate that syn overexpression in midbrain dopaminergic neurons is sufficient to drive cognitive decline. Our early-stage PD model offers a temporal window to dissect cellular and circuits mechanisms underlying non-motor manifestations of PD.

item.title: Neural mechanisms of lightness constancy
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Didehvar, F., Vanstiphout, R., Cavanagh, P., Franken, T. P.
Object-specific variables are entangled in sensory input. For example, lightness, whether a surface is white or black, not only depends on the surface reflectance but also on the incident illumination. The brain must thus perform inference to achieve a reliable percept of lightness irrespective of illumination (lightness constancy). Whether this results from simple luminance contrast operations early in the visual system or computations at higher levels remains unresolved. We find that neural lightness signals only appear in the extragranular layers of cortical Area V4, and dominate for shadow regions, as opposed to the comparison of local and surrounding luminance (simultaneous contrast). This suggests that lightness is computed downstream from simultaneous contrast, ruling out simple low-level mechanisms, and instead supporting mid-level anchoring theory.

item.title: Neural competition predicts speech production advantages in congenital amusia
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Wang, Y., Liu, M., Jin, Z., Huyang, S., Guo, N., Zhan, J., Lian, Q., Su, C., Liu, Q., Huang, S., Ji, Y., Wu, D.
Mental health research has traditionally been deficit-focused, and cognitive advantages in mental conditions have almost always been documented retrospectively. Here we propose and test an a priori pathway for predicting such advantages from a condition's impaired neural basis, neural competition and brain-mind associations. Using congenital amusia (CA), a neurodevelopmental disorder with a well-defined deficit in right frontotemporal circuit (FTC), as a model, we predicted that interhemispheric competition would release the left homologue from inhibition, conferring advantages in speech production. Two independent studies, multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral testing, confirmed this prediction: MRI revealed right FTC impairment alongside competitive-like benefits of the left FTC in CA; and CA showed speech production advantages with intact episodic memory and constrained music learning. These findings provide the first empirical demonstration that cognitive advantages can be predicted in advance and then verified, offering a principled, mechanism-based alternative to the deficit-focused paradigm.

item.title: HBRAN Stage 19: the complete self-model layer, with meta-reasoning as a monitor
item.description:
Relevance: 24% | Source: SocArXiv
klaus syha
Registered test of the recurrent workspace architecture HBRAN (K. Syha, The Nat and the Architecture, v5.6, Chapter 21 and Appendix G). Configuration M adds the fourth component of the self-model layer's specification, meta-reasoning, to the configuration of record K, as a monitor: a confidence head reads the self-model without shaping it, and the gate reads its estimate of the system's own error without the task shaping it. Fresh seeds 191 to 198, on an encyclopaedic corpus and on a constructed corpus of ordered procedures. Eleven predictions (M1 to M11) with decision rules: those of the registered test of K, and M11, that the self-assessed error tracks the actual error. Exploratory pilots (stated in the PDF) showed M as stable as K but its estimate uncalibrated; M11 is therefore expected to fail. The attached PDF gives the full registration; the attached manifest the SHA-256 hashes of the frozen code. The run starts only after this registration.

item.title: Does Motor Inhibition Persist Beyond the Stop-Signal Reaction Time? A Paired-Pulse TMS Investigation
item.description:
Relevance: 23% | Source: SocArXiv
Jan Wessel et al.
The ability to rapidly cancel an ongoing action is a fundamental component of cognitive control and is commonly investigated using the stop-signal task (SST). According to the horse-race model, successful stopping occurs when a stopping process finishes before the competing Go process. Although this process cannot be directly observed behaviorally, its latency can be estimated using the stop-signal reaction time (SSRT; Logan & Cowan, 1984). Converging neuroscientific evidence suggests that inhibitory activity may continue beyond SSRT (Boucher et al., 2007; Wessel & Aron, 2015; Raud & Huster, 2017; De Havas et al., 2025; Soh et al., 2026). For example, electrophysiological studies have demonstrated stopping-related activity extending beyond SSRT, while recent investigations have identified sustained motor suppression and subthalamic nucleus (STN) activity following action cancellation. Together, these findings suggest that the neural processes associated with stopping may persist beyond the estimated completion of behavioral inhibition. However, whether intracortical inhibitory mechanisms within primary motor cortex (M1) remain engaged during this period is not yet established. The present study aims to investigate the temporal dynamics of motor inhibition by combining the SST with single-pulse (SP) and paired-pulse (PP) transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). SP TMS will be used to assess corticospinal excitability (CSE), while PP TMS will measure short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), which is associated with GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibitory mechanisms within M1 (Kujirai et al., 1993; Ziemann et al., 1996). Participants will complete a manual SST while motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) are recorded using electromyography (EMG). TMS will be delivered at multiple time points, including SSRT − 50 ms, SSRT + 100 ms, and SSRT + 200 ms on Stop trials. By comparing successful Stop trials with temporally matched Go trials and active-baseline measurements, we will examine whether reductions in CSE and increases in SICI persist beyond the estimated completion of stopping. We hypothesize that successful stopping will be associated with reduced corticospinal excitability and increased intracortical inhibition, particularly at post-SSRT time points. We will also explore how these physiological effects change over time to characterize the duration of stopping-related inhibition. By distinguishing changes in overall corticospinal excitability from intracortical inhibitory processes, this study aims to clarify whether motor inhibition remains actively engaged after an action has been successfully cancelled and contribute to our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control.

item.title: The Role of Specific Cognitive Skills in Solving Elementary Mathematics Word Problems
item.description:
Relevance: 23% | Source: SocArXiv
Dania Carr et al.
Word problem performance is associated with a range of cognitive skills such as working memory, language comprehension, fluid reasoning, spatial reasoning, and inhibitory control (e.g., Fuchs et al., 2018; Fung & Swanson, 2017; Tam et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2011; Lubin et al., 2013), likely because solving word problems requires skills beyond simple calculation, such as maintaining and integrating information, inhibiting irrelevant content, and mapping linguistic information onto mathematical representations. Most studies that have examined the role of domain general cognitive skills in mathematics have focused on a limited subset, have examined these skills in isolation (e.g., working memory or spatial skills alone; Passolunghi & Siegel, 2001; Tam et al., 2019), or both. Thus, it is an open question which specific cognitive predictors explain the most variance in mathematics performance when considered simultaneously alongside other domain-general cognitive skills. The current study addresses this gap by testing the contributions of multiple cognitive skills that have been associated with word problem success in past research within a single analytic framework, allowing for a more comprehensive assessment. As an exploratory analysis, we also investigate whether there are gender differences in word problem performance and if so, whether these gender differences are explained by differences in particular cognitive skills.
